background.definition: Pemphigus is 1 of 4 major groups of autoimmune blistering diseases (AIBDs) characterized by cutaneous or mucous membrane flaccid blisters, erosions, aphthae, or crusts caused by autoantibodies against the intercellular junctions. Pemphigoid, another group of AIBDs, is characterized by cutaneous or mucous membrane tense blisters, erosions, plaques, papules, or scars caused by autoantibodies against the hemidesmosomal anchoring complex. The 2 other AIBD groups consist of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita and dermatitis herpetiformis. (This chapter mainly focuses on pemphigus and pemphigoid.)

list.listitem: Pemphigus worldwide: 0.076 to 2.7/100,000 persons/y.
Pemphigus in United States: 0.42/100,000 persons/y.
Pemphigoid in France: 1.04/100,000 persons/y.
The incidence of bullous pemphigoid was 7.6 per 100,000 person-years in the UK from 1998 to 2017. The incidence was increasing over time, as was prevalence.
Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common AIBD in the Western hemisphere.
Autoantibodies to specific structural proteins of the skin (ie, autoantigens) (see ).
Associations have been found with use of aldosterone antagonists (OR 1.8), dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors OR 1.9), anticholinergics (OR, 3.1), and dopaminergic medications (OR, 2.0).

Pemphigus is caused by autoantibodies against desmogleins, which are structural proteins of intercellular junctions resulting in loss of cell-to-cell adhesion in the epithelium (acantholysis) and consequent intraepidermal blistering.

Pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies aimed at proteins of the hemidesmosomal anchoring complex such as BP180 and BP230 resulting in loss of cell-to-matrix adhesion and consequent subepidermal blistering.

Autoantibodies are present during active disease and, in certain AIBD subtypes, may disappear during remission. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) and indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) demonstrate tissue-bound and circulating serum autoantibodies, respectively. Immunoassays, which include immunoblotting, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and immunoprecipitation, are highly accurate tests that identify involved autoantigens.
Epidermolysis bullosa is a rare genetic blistering skin condition that is cause by mutations including COL7A1, a gene encoding collagen and others.

If either direct Nikolsky sign or marginal Nikolsky sign is present on physical examination, pemphigus is very likely. C
The presence of intraepidermal acantholysis on histologic evaluation of mucosal lesions is highly suggestive of pemphigus; the presence of subepidermal bullae is highly suggestive of pemphigoid. C

Demonstration of tissue-bound autoantibodies through DIF microscopy of perilesional skin or mucosa provides strong evidence in favor of pemphigus and pemphigoid. Similarly, demonstration of circulating serum autoantibodies through IIF microscopy provides strong evidence in favor of pemphigus and pemphigoid.C

Accurate identification of specific autoantigens for each AIBD group and subtype, through use of immunoassays (eg, immunoprecipitation, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and immunoblotting), is the final crucial step in the diagnosis of pemphigus and pemphigoid. C
Consider epidermolysis bullosa in a neonate with fragile, blistering skin.

list.listitem: See for the revised MWHJ diagnostic criteria for pemphigus. In the Japanese population, these criteria are very sensitive (94.1%) and highly specific (100%).
Consider a diagnosis of pemphigus or pemphigoid in patients with cutaneous or mucosal blisters, erosions, papules, plaques, or crusts.
Conduct a diagnostic evaluation for pemphigus in patients with multiple cutaneous or mucous membrane flaccid blisters, erosions, aphthae, or crusts.
The presence of direct and marginal Nikolsky signs provides strong evidence in favor of pemphigus (especially pemphigus vulgaris).
Conduct a diagnostic evaluation for pemphigoid in patients with cutaneous or mucous membrane tense blisters, erosions, plaques, or papules, with or without scarring.
British Academy of Dermatology (BAD) guidelines (2017) recommend perilesional skin biopsies for direct immunofluorescence (DIF) and histology as the primary diagnostic modality.

Despite its modest accuracy as a screening tool for pemphigus and pemphigoid, histologic evaluation (using light microscopy) remains an important initial workup due to its wide availability and affordability. Demonstration of intraepidermal acantholysis on histologic evaluation of mucosal lesions (obtained by punch biopsy and transported in formaldehyde) provides strong evidence in favor of pemphigus. Likewise, the presence of subepidermal bullae on histologic examination of mucosal lesions provides strong evidence in favor of pemphigoid.

The demonstration of tissue-bound autoantibodies through DIF microscopy of perilesional skin or mucosa (obtained by punch biopsy and snap frozen or placed in special transport medium) provides strong evidence of pemphigus. DIF is also useful as a test to rule in pemphigoid when positive. In contrast, negative DIF provides moderate evidence against pemphigus and modest evidence against pemphigoid.
A retrospective single-center study demonstrated that multiple and repeated mucosal biopsies for DIF increased the sensitivity for mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) diagnosis.
The demonstration of circulating serum autoantibodies through IIF microscopy provides strong evidence in favor of pemphigus, whereas negative IIF provides moderate evidence against pemphigus.

A study identified 1125 patients with suspected pemphigoid who had all undergone DIF microscopy, IIF on a salt-split skin substrate (IIF-SSS), and at least one immunoserologic test. The prevalence of pemphigoid diagnosis was approximately 30%, of whom 1 in 5 had non-bullous disease. They found that DIF was highly sensitive (88%) while IIF was highly specific (99.9%). Thus, a negative DIF helps rule out the diagnosis, while a positive IIF rules it in. BP180 NC16A did not add diagnostic value.

Once the diagnosis has been established by histologic examination, DIF, and IIF, the final step in diagnosing pemphigus and pemphigoid is establishing the specific subtype (ie, pemphigus vulgaris vs. pemphigus foliaceus, bullous pemphigoid vs. MMP) by accurate identification of specific autoantigens through use of immunoassays. Given their extremely accurate test properties, immunoassays may soon replace IIF in the evaluation of AIBD.
Once the diagnosis is confirmed and before starting treatment, consider obtaining CBC with differential, BUN, electrolytes, liver function testing, lipids, and urinalysis.

Detection of specific pemphigus autoantigens in serum, confirmed by desmoglein (Dsg) 1 and Dsg3 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), is an accurate test for pemphigus. Used independently, Dsg1 and Dsg3 ELISAs are accurate tests for pemphigus vulgaris (PV), while Dsg1 is accurate for pemphigus foliaceus (PF).

Tests specific for bullous pemphigoid (BP) include BP180 and BP230. Either one being abnormal is strong evidence for BP, while if both are negative it is very unlikely. Indirect immunofluorescence IgG when tested on salt split skin can distinguish between BP and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA), but is less sensitive in patients with localized disease.
DIF is most sensitive and specific for pemphigoid gestationis, while serum tests are less sensitive. Laminin 5 ELISA is moderately accurate for MMP.

If epidermolysis bullosa is suspected in a neonate, obtain a skin biopsy with immunofluorescence mapping and genetic testing for specific mutations. Transmission electron microscopy may be helpful if initial testing is inconclusive.
Suspect pemphigus or pemphigoid in patients with cutaneous or mucosal blisters, erosions, papules, plaques, or crusts.
Biopsy with histologic evaluation, DIF microscopy to detect tissue-bound autoantibodies, and detection of circulating serum autoantibodies are central to the diagnosis.
Systemic corticosteroids are the best established treatment for pemphigus, combined with adjuvant immunosuppressive therapy (rituximab, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil).C

Strong topical corticosteroids and lower doses of oral corticosteroids appear safe and effective for BP, A in combination with adjuvant immunosuppressive therapy (methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil). C
Corticosteroid plus cyclophosphamide may be beneficial for severe MMP (ie, with eye involvement). For mild-to-moderate disease, corticosteroid plus dapsone may be sufficient. B
Rituximab induces B cell depletion and can achieve prolonged clinical remission in pemphigus patients.B

The main goals of therapy for pemphigus and pemphigoid are to induce disease remission, maintain adequate disease control using the lowest drug doses, and, whenever possible, withdraw treatment from patients with prolonged clinical remission.

Systemic corticosteroids are the best established treatment. Starting doses of prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for most patients, with 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg in milder cases, are recommended. This can be increased in 50% to 100% increments weekly if not effective (ie, persistent blistering). Once remission is achieved, taper slowly with a goal of 10 mg per day or less.

Second line therapy in the event of treatment failure includes one of the adjuvant drugs such as rituximab, azathioprine, or mycophenolate mofetil. However, the 2017 BAD guidelines recommend combining corticosteroids with adjuvant therapy such as rituximab using the rheumatoid arthritis protocol, azathioprine 2-3 mg/kg/day, or mycophenolate mofetil 2-3 grams/day.
Predictors of relapse after treatment with rituximab include a Pemphigus Disease Area Index (PDAI) score > 44, DSG1 antibodies > 20 IU/mL, and DSG3 antibodies > 130 IU/mL.
Third line therapy choices include cyclophosphamide, immunoadsorption, intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG), methotrexate, and plasmapherresis.

A trial randomized 135 patients with moderately severe PV to IV rituximab (1000 mg on days 1, 15, 168 and 182) or oral mycophenolate mofetil (2 gm/day), along with a tapering course of an oral glucocorticoid. At one year, a complete sustained response was seen more often in the rituximab group (40% vs 10%, p < 0.001, NNT = 3).There were also fewer disease flares in the rituximab group (5 versus 44, p < 0.001); serious adverse events were similar between groups.

In patients with new PV, adding oral dexamethasone pulse therapy to conventional treatment (ie, systemic corticosteroids) has not been well studied, but BAD guidelines recommend considering it in patients not responding to 1 mg/kg/day. Topical epidermal growth factor can also significantly reduce healing time of skin lesions in patients with PV.
Bullous pemphigoid (BP)

Very potent topical corticosteroids are effective and safe for patients with BP. For patients with more extensive disease, the usefulness of full body steroid application is limited by potential systemic absorption and the tediousness of whole body cream application.

Daily full body application of clobetasol propionate cream is as effective (in the short-term), may lead to lower severe adverse events (short-term), and may lead to lower one-year mortality (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53-1.01; 1 study, 341 patients; low-certainty evidence) compared to oral prednisone.
Full body application of clobetasol propionate cream at milder doses of 10 to 30 g/day (tapered over 4 months) appears as effective and safe as the standard dose of 40 g/day (tapered over 12 months).

An updated Cochrane review concluded that a lower starting dose of prednisolone of 0.5 mg/kg/day appears as effective in controlling disease activity and may be safer (eg, less adverse events and lower mortality) than doses higher than 0.75 mg/kg/day for most patients with BP.

Oral doxycycline 200 mg/day is less effective in controlling disease activity but improves one-year mortality (NNT = 14) compared to oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day for patients with BP. It improves quality of life and is associated with less severe or life-threatening adverse events.

The following interventions for BP have uncertain effectiveness: azathioprine plus corticosteroids, dapsone plus corticosteroids, dapsone plus sulfonamides, anti-inflammatory antibiotics (tetracycline) plus nicotinamide (vitamin B3), methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, topical tacrolimus, IVIG, plasmapheresis, and immunoapheresis.

Low-dose interleukin 2 (IL-2) may be an effective adjunctive therapy for moderate to severe BP, possibly lowering the total amount of corticosteroid use. However, larger, more rigorous trials are needed.

There is limited evidence that MMP involving the eyes responds best to treatment with cyclophosphamide combined with corticosteroids. However, MMP with mild-to-moderate inflammatory activity responds to dapsone in most participants and may therefore be best treated with dapsone due to its lower side effect profile compared with cyclophosphamide.
A topical herpes simplex virus type 1 vectored gene therapy (beremagene geperpavec) improved wound healing at 6 months compared with placebo (67% vs 22%, p = .002, NNT = 2).

Oleogel-S10 (birch triterpenes) is a topical gel with potential antibacterial, antiviral and anti-inflammatory effects. In a randomized trial with 223 patients with a wound, closure occurred more often with Oleogel-S10 (41.3% vs 28.9%, p = 0.013, NNT = 8).

Recommendations regarding care of neonates with epidermolysis bullosa including avoiding use of clamps that can be traumatic, covering any birth trauma with film or nonadherent dressing, use a padded layer if stimulation for breathing is required, use extra padding in incubators, do not attach hospital ID so it touches skin, and apply emollient to catheter tips used for suction.

Given the rarity of AIBD, its potentially life-threatening nature, and the high morbidity associated with it, patients suspected of having the disorder should be referred immediately to a specialist (eg, dermatologist, dentist, oral surgeon, or ophthalmologist).

Induction of complete and durable remissions in most patients with pemphigus is an achievable goal; the proportion of patients in whom this can be achieved increases steadily with time, and therapy can be discontinued in approximately 75% of patients after 10 years. C

Order DIF microscopy in patients with pemphigus who are in clinical remission (for at least 6 months) for whom treatment discontinuation is being entertained. A positive DIF test precisely identifies those who will relapse, whereas a negative test accurately predicts those who will stay in remission (PPV = 100%, NPV = 77%). C
The natural history of both treated and untreated BP is persistent disease with eventual remission, usually within 5 years. C
Predictors of relapse after treatment with rituximab include a Pemphigus Disease Area Index (PDAI) score > 44, DSG1 antibodies > 20 IU/mL, and DSG3 antibodies > 130 IU/mL.

In contrast, the natural history of MMP is highly variable, and the disease often takes a protracted course. Localized oral MMP may remain stable for years in the absence of aggressive therapy while rapidly progressive ocular involvement may develop despite treatment with immunosuppressants. C

For BP, autoantibody titers (ie, BP180) correlate well with disease activity, whereas IIF does not. For pemphigoid gestationis and MMP, IIF is often negative and not useful in disease monitoring. Studies are needed to explore the usefulness of these tools in monitoring therapy and in assisting in decisions pertaining to treatment discontinuation. C

A retrospective cohort study of 79 patients with pemphigus vulgaris and 16 with pemphigus foliaceus found that worse prognosis was associated with a younger age at onset, a higher initial intercellular antibody titer, and a higher anti-Dsg3 level.

A systemic review and meta-analysis did not find an association with BP and overall malignancy. A pooled analysis of cross-sectional studies found a significant association with hematologic malignancies but there was a paucity of well-designed studies. BP has been associated with neurodegenerative disorders such as dementia and Parkinson's disease. Gliptins, a class of diabetes medications, has been associated with drug-induced BP.
A large cohort study using UK electronic health records found increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.54) especially in the 2 years after diagnosis (HR 2.96).
BP is the most common AIBD in the elderly.
Pemphigoid gestationis, although rare, is the only known AIBD associated with pregnancy.
Linear IgA disease of childhood (or chronic bullous disease of childhood) is the most common AIBD in children.

feature.caption: Revised Ministry of Welfare and Health of Japan (MWHJ) Diagnostic Criteria for Pemphigus.

list.listitem: Clinical findings Multiple, flaccid blisters that easily erode Progressive, intractable erosions and crust after blisters Mucosal noninfectious erosions or aphthae Nikolsky phenomenon
Histopathologic examination Intraepidermal blister caused by epidermal cell dissociation (acantholysis)

Immuno-histochemical examination Diagnosis of pemphigus can be made if the patient is: In vivo bound intercellular IgG class autoantibodies (direct immunofluorescence microscopy) Circulating anti-intercellular IgG class autoantibodies (indirect immunofluorescence microscopy)
